name: Marco Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Marco. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions or any political party, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me is confidential and won't carry your name. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a plastics plant out by the ring road that makes clips and trim pieces for car dashboards. I run two injection moulding presses, so I load the colour pellets into the hopper, watch the cycle, pull the parts off the conveyor, check them against the sample board and bin the ones with flash or short shots. Short shot means the plastic didn't fill the mould all the way, and on a cold Monday morning you get loads of them. I'm on rotating shifts, which my body still hasn't forgiven me for after three years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Three years. What brought you there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I had a little café for nine years, sandwiches and coffee near the bus station, and it went under after the rent doubled. I was 40, two kids, Leila doing extra nursing shifts to cover us, so I took the first steady job with a contract. I'm still learning the setters' side, how to change a mould and tweak the temperatures, and the older guys are patient with me, mostly. What I like is that the money comes in on the same day every month, which after the café feels like a miracle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what my mate Dev says, it was another bubble, like crypto. Someone made a lot of money selling it and the rest of us carried on making dashboard clips. At work it'd be a joke for a week and then nobody would mention it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit relieved and a bit disappointed. I've used the chatbot to write a letter to the council about our bins and it was handy. If it's only that, fine, my job is safe and I keep climbing slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same plan as now. I'd keep asking Raj, the setter, to show me mould changes so I can get the setter's rate in a couple of years, and keep putting a bit by. We've got about four months saved, which is the most we've ever had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. It's the world I already know how to live in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI tools now and then. Where does that fit in now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Little things. I asked it to explain what a hot runner was before Raj showed me, so I didn't look stupid. And Sami uses it for homework, which I keep an eye on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope the plant puts its energy into instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safety, and pay. We've had two near misses on the presses this year, and the new hires get the worst shifts. If they're not buying robots, they can spend it on us.

S0.say: It was another bubble, like crypto, and people would joke about it at work for a week. Someone made money selling it and everyone else carried on making dashboard clips.
S0.think: He's relieved and a little disappointed, because he's found the chatbot handy for letters. If that's all it is, his job is safe and he keeps climbing slowly toward setter.
S0.do: Keeps learning mould changes from the setter to reach the setter's rate in a couple of years. Keeps adding to the roughly four months of savings the family has built up.
S0.feel: Calm, because it's the world he already knows how to live in.
S0.quote: If they're not buying robots, they can spend it on us.
S0.fieldNote: After losing his café, Marco measures security by whether the pay arrives on time, and a flat AI future suits him. He uses AI casually and practically, like explaining a term before a colleague does. He quickly turns the question toward workplace safety and fair shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, this is real now, so the union needs a seat at the table before the machines arrive, not after. I'd say workers should get training on paid time and a share of what's saved. I'd post that in the works group chat, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my presses are exactly the kind of thing that gets a robot arm and a camera. Pulling parts and binning bad ones is the easy bit to automate. So I'd better become the guy who sets the machines, not the guy who unloads them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager straight out for the setter training and put my name down first. I'd look up the evening course at the college for basic maintenance and controls, which I think is two nights a week. And I'd start using the AI tools more, like getting it to quiz me on fault codes, once I saw the others doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. But I've started over once, so I know it doesn't kill you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the plant would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pauline on nights, she's been there twenty years and she's brilliant, but she won't touch a touchscreen. And the young agency lads, because they're the easiest to let go. I'd want the union to fight for both, not just people like me who'll adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get on the setter course. What if the plant doesn't offer one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd pay for the college one myself, if it's a few hundred. I'd talk to Leila first, because it's our savings and her overtime. But it's cheaper than losing the job.

S1.say: This is real, so the union needs a seat at the table before the machines arrive. Workers should get training on paid time and a share of what's saved, and he'd post that in the works group chat.
S1.think: His job of pulling and binning parts is the easiest bit to automate, so he needs to become the person who sets the machines. Unloading them won't last.
S1.do: Asks his manager for setter training and signs up for a two-night-a-week college course in maintenance and controls, paying himself if needed. Starts using AI to quiz himself on fault codes.
S1.feel: Uneasy, but steadied by having started over once already.
S1.quote: I'd better become the guy who sets the machines, not the guy who unloads them.
S1.fieldNote: Marco pairs a collective public message with a personal plan to climb out of the most exposed task. He worries about colleagues who can't or won't adapt, and wants the union to protect them too. His past café failure works as proof to himself that he can survive a restart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in, now, with income support and a tax on the companies that use it. You can't put millions of people out of work in two years and say 'good luck'. I'd go on the marches, and I'd take Sami, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd be in trouble. Leila's job might hold longer because people want a nurse's hand, but not forever. I'd be out with the first wave, probably, because I'm the junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop all the extras and push every spare penny into savings to stretch the four months to six. I'd sign up with the union for whatever campaign they ran for income support. And I'd look for any work near people, like care work, because that might last a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I keep seeing the café's shutters coming down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, what happens to your plan to become a setter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's gone, basically. Why learn to set a press when a robot sets itself by 2028? That's the part that gets me, I'd finally have a plan and it'd be pointless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would money look like at home in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd live on Leila's wage and the savings and cut to the bone, no holiday, no car upgrade, the kids' swimming club maybe. We'd call the bank early about the mortgage. Last time with the café I waited too long to ask for help, and I won't do that again.

S2.say: Governments need to step in now with income support and a tax on companies that use AGI. He'd march, and take his son, because millions can't be put out of work in two years.
S2.think: He'd likely be in the first wave out because he's junior, and his wife's nursing job would only hold for a while. He thinks the family would be in real trouble.
S2.do: Cuts all extras and pushes spare money into savings to stretch four months to six. Joins union campaigns for income support, calls the bank early about the mortgage and looks for care work near people.
S2.feel: Frightened, with memories of the café shutters coming down.
S2.quote: I'd finally have a plan and it'd be pointless.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture breaks the one plan he had, which hurts him more than the job loss itself. He has learned from the café to ask for help early. His politics turn from union bargaining to state action and a tax on the firms using AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years, so let's use them, with retraining money, shorter weeks and some kind of basic income ready to go. I'd say it at union meetings and I'd vote that way. I'd try not to sound like the end of the world, because people switch off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 48, which is young enough to do something else but old enough that nobody will hand it to me. I think I'd have about three years of real work left at the plant. So I'd use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the evening course straight away and then look at moving towards maintenance or care, whichever looks safer. I'd save hard, at least two hundred a month, and pay a lump off the mortgage. I'd ask the AI tools what's likely to last, and ask actual people too, because I don't trust it fully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do about it. That's better than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change for you, compared to the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time for the kids, mostly. Sami would be 17, Nora 13, so I'd have a bit of time to work out their next steps too. And for us, time to get the mortgage down so a smaller wage could still cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still bother with the setter route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a year or two, because it pays more while it lasts. Every extra pound is a pound in the savings pot. But I wouldn't think of it as my future anymore.

S3.say: There are a few years, so use them with retraining money, shorter weeks and a basic income ready to go. He'd say it at union meetings and try not to sound like the world is ending.
S3.think: At 48 he's young enough to change but old enough that nobody will hand him the chance. He reckons he'd have about three years of real work left at the plant.
S3.do: Starts the evening course straight away and aims toward maintenance or care. Saves at least two hundred a month, pays a lump off the mortgage and checks AI tools and real people for which jobs last.
S3.feel: Anxious but with something to do about it, which is better than the fast picture.
S3.quote: Every extra pound is a pound in the savings pot. But I wouldn't think of it as my future anymore.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets him treat the setter rate as a short-term earner rather than a career. He thinks about the timing of his children's ages and the mortgage. He uses AI for advice but checks it against people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it fairly, if anyone bothers. Shorter week, retraining paid for by the companies, and a share in what the robots make. I'd keep going on about it, Leila says I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like a career's worth of time. I'd get to setter, maybe maintenance, put real money away and be 53 at the end of it. I'm not calm, but I'm not scared either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the setter route as planned, then the maintenance course in year two or three. I'd save steadily and put a bit into the pension. And I'd get more involved in the union, maybe become a rep, because these years are when the deal gets made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the kind you can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you tell your kids to plan their careers differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. Sami wants to be a mechanic, and I'd tell him to aim for the people side, like running a garage or teaching it. Nora's into art, which I used to think was a risk and now I'm not sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union to win in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A share of the savings for every job a robot takes, written down. Notice of two years minimum. And paid training, not 'do it in your own time'.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time to do it fairly, with a shorter week, company-paid retraining and a share in what the robots make. He'd keep making the case, as his wife says he already does.
S4.think: Ten years feels like a career's worth of time, enough to reach setter or maintenance and put money away. He'd be 53 at the end, not calm but not scared either.
S4.do: Follows the setter route, then a maintenance course in year two or three. Saves steadily, adds to his pension, steers his son toward the people side of mechanics and becomes more active in the union, possibly as a rep.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but the kind of unease he can live with.
S4.quote: Nora's into art, which I used to think was a risk and now I'm not sure.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he returns to his original ladder and adds union work on top. His advice to his children shows his thinking shifting about what counts as a safe career. He sees these years as the window when the deal gets made.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my whole plan becomes pointless overnight and so does half the country's. What would help is income support that's ready before it hits, not two years of forms, and the mortgage people being told to give families breathing room. And training that's paid, in work time, so I'm not choosing between learning and feeding the kids.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about pride. When the café shut I couldn't look at the bus station for a year. People think losing a job is about money, and it is, but it's also walking past the place and feeling like you failed.

headlineQuote: When the café shut I couldn't look at the bus station for a year.
portrait: Marco Usman, 43, runs two injection moulding presses making dashboard clips, three years into factory work after his café went under. He uses AI now and then and leans on the union and the state for fairness. A flat AI future suits him, and steady change pushes him to climb from unloading machines to setting them. Fast AGI wrecks that plan and frightens him, but with five or ten years he goes back to retraining, saving and union work, while rethinking what he tells his kids.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his one plan to become a setter would become pointless overnight, along with many other people's.
whatWouldHelp: Income support ready before the change hits, breathing room on mortgages, and paid training in work time so he doesn't have to choose between learning and feeding his kids.
